intervals.note: Start is a lower bound: the August 2018 science-goals paper says SO is "being built"; no source states when construction began. End: the 2024 press release says the "completion of the observatory's main construction phase coincided with Simons' 86th birthday on April 25"; the year (2024) is inferred from the release date (3 June 2024) and Jim Simons's death on 10 May 2024, which the release dates "a few weeks later".
intervals.quote: The Simons Observatory (SO) is a new cosmic microwave background experiment being built on Cerro Toco in Chile, due to begin observations in the early 2020s.

intervals.locator: Simons Foundation press release of 3 June 2024, paragraph 1
intervals.note: Start is the press-release date: the release says the observatory "just completed its main construction phase" and observers "have begun searching"; earlier engineering or first-light observations (the SATs) are not sourced here. Status as of 26 October 2026: the Simons Foundation release of 22 October 2026 says "the Simons Observatory in Chile is completely online and conducting science operations".
intervals.quote: From a vantage point high in the Chilean Andes, cosmologists with the Simons Observatory have begun searching for evidence of what happened in the minuscule fraction of a second that followed the Big Bang.

physics_goals.quote: Our key science goals are to characterize the primordial perturbations, measure the number of relativistic species and the mass of neutrinos, test for deviations from a cosmological constant, improve our understanding of galaxy evolution, and constrain the duration of reionization.
physics_goals.value: Characterize the primordial perturbations, measure the number of relativistic species and the neutrino mass, test for deviations from a cosmological constant, and improve understanding of galaxy evolution and reionization.

summary.plain: A set of four telescopes on a 5190-metre Chilean mountain, with about 98,000 detectors, that maps the Big Bang afterglow deeply and quickly. It aims to detect the polarization pattern of cosmic inflation and was reported fully online in October 2026.
summary.technical: CMB observatory on Cerro Toco (5190 m) in the Parque Astronómico Atacama: 6 m Large Aperture Telescope and three 0.5 m SATs (27-280 GHz, ~98,000 detectors), built by a collaboration formed from ACT and the Simons Array; construction to April 2024, observing since June 2024, LAT first light 22 February 2025, fully online October 2026.
